column2: Stasis in a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle (and atria in AF) causes mural thrombus and embolism; anticoagulate for AF or documented LV thrombus.
S3 reflects rapid filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle with high filling pressure (gallop rhythm). Opening snap = MS; pericardial knock = constriction.
DCM causes: alcohol, haemochromatosis, myocarditis, genetic, peripartum, anthracyclines, tachycardia. Hypertension causes concentric LVH and HFpEF, so is least likely.
Beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) mutations classically cause HCM. Alcohol, pregnancy and persistent tachycardia cause DCM (the last two may reverse).
With COPD and IHD together, a gallop rhythm (S3) is the most specific sign that breathlessness is from LV failure with high filling pressure.
By LVEF: HFrEF ≤ 40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥ 50% with raised filling pressures. High-output failure is a separate category.
ACC/AHA stages: A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C structural disease with symptoms, D refractory. NYHA classes grade symptoms separately.
CRT (biventricular pacing) for HFrEF with EF ≤ 35%, LBBB and QRS ≥ 150 ms despite optimal therapy restores synchrony and improves EF and survival.
Long-standing hypertension causes LVH: tall voltages (S V1 + R V5/6 > 35 mm) with lateral ST–T 'strain'. RVH suggests pulmonary hypertension.
Exertional fatigue and syncope with familial sudden death in a teenager is HCM, the commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes; ECG and echo first.
The HCM murmur comes from dynamic LVOT obstruction (septal hypertrophy plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve); it does not radiate to the carotids.
Echo confirms HCM: unexplained wall thickness ≥ 15 mm (often septal), SAM and an outflow gradient. MRI and Holter refine risk.
Syncope in HCM is usually from ventricular arrhythmia or a surge in outflow obstruction; unexplained syncope is a major sudden-death risk factor favouring an ICD.
Orthopnoea is breathlessness soon after lying flat (venous redistribution), relieved by sitting up. PND wakes the patient after hours of sleep.
RV infarction with inferior MI: hypotension, raised JVP, hepatomegaly and clear lungs. Give IV fluids and avoid nitrates and diuretics.
Frank–Starling: stroke volume and output rise with ventricular filling (preload) up to a plateau; in heart failure the curve is flat, so extra filling causes congestion.
Low output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system: salt/water retention, vasoconstriction and remodelling — the targets of ACEi/ARNI, MRAs and beta-blockers.
DCM is dilatation (often biventricular) with thin walls and systolic dysfunction not explained by loading or coronary disease. Septal thickening = HCM.
Heavy alcohol (> 80 g/day for years) is a common, reversible cause of DCM. SCN5A mutations cause Brugada and long QT3.
HCM: asymmetric LVH with disproportionate septal thickening (septum/posterior wall > 1.3), myocyte disarray and dynamic outflow obstruction in ~two-thirds.
Transplantation is for stage D heart failure with poor quality of life despite optimal drug and device therapy and no contraindications; LVAD is an alternative.
Sudden death in HCM is from VT/VF arising in fibrotic myocardium, often on exertion; risk is scored (ESC HCM Risk-SCD) and high-risk patients get an ICD.
Beta-blockers reduce total and sudden death in HFrEF (as do MRAs and ARNI); consider an ICD if EF stays ≤ 35%. Verapamil is harmful; screen the family.
ST elevation, normal coronaries and apical ballooning in a postmenopausal woman after emotional stress is takotsubo cardiomyopathy; LV function usually recovers.
Loop diuretics relieve symptoms but do not improve survival. Bisoprolol, enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone and SGLT2i reduce mortality.
Heart failure with high EF and a pseudo-infarct ECG (low voltages) in an elderly woman suggests restrictive (amyloid) cardiomyopathy.
Thyroid disease causes heart failure: thyrotoxicosis gives high-output failure and AF; hypothyroidism a dilated heart. Check TFTs in all new heart failure.
HCM is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance (MYH7, MYBPC3); screen first-degree relatives with ECG and echo ± genetic testing.
Hypertensive pulmonary oedema: oxygen/CPAP, IV nitrates and IV furosemide. Dobutamine is for cardiogenic shock and only raises oxygen demand here.
Anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity is cumulative, dose-dependent and largely irreversible. Alcohol, haemochromatosis and thyroid DCM can improve.
Pulsus alternans (alternating strong and weak beats in regular rhythm, independent of respiration) indicates severe LV systolic dysfunction.
S4 needs atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it cannot occur in AF. S3, reversed splitting (LBBB) and Kussmaul's sign all fit.
Thick 'sparkling' myocardium with biatrial enlargement and preserved EF suggests amyloidosis: first exclude AL with serum/urine electrophoresis and free light chains.
NSVT in heart failure predicts higher mortality, but antiarrhythmic suppression does not help (class I harmful, CAST); optimise HF therapy and electrolytes.
Comfortable at rest but symptoms on less than ordinary activity (e.g. a short walk) is NYHA class III.
Heart failure with warm peripheries, tachycardia, exophthalmos and tremor is thyrotoxic high-output failure: beta-blocker, diuretic and treat the thyroid.
In HFrEF angiotensin II, noradrenaline, natriuretic peptides and TNF rise, but SR calcium uptake falls (SERCA2a down-regulated), impairing relaxation.
BNP rises with age, female sex, CKD, AF, PE, sepsis and ACS. Obesity lowers BNP, so a 'normal' value does not exclude heart failure in obese patients.
Correcting hypoxaemia relieves hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and lowers RV afterload. High PEEP, large tidal volumes and hypercapnia raise it.
No drug has convincingly reduced mortality in HFpEF; SGLT2i reduce the combined endpoint mainly via fewer admissions. Treat congestion and comorbidities.
'Warm and wet': start an IV loop diuretic (at least the oral dose). Inotropes are for 'cold' low-output states; ultrafiltration for diuretic resistance.
Nesiritide (recombinant BNP) lowers wedge pressure faster than nitrates but causes hypotension and did not improve outcomes (ASCEND-HF).
In cardiogenic shock output falls and sympathetic vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance (cool peripheries); mixed venous saturation falls.
Beta-blocker or ACEi first gives similar outcomes (CIBIS III); start all four pillars early in low doses and titrate to target.
Adding an ARB or aliskiren to ACEi + MRA raises hyperkalaemia and renal risk without benefit; SGLT2i need caution in type 1 diabetes (ketoacidosis), so no change.
